newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka lawmakers urge talks with Tamil rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka lawmakers urge talks with Tamil rebels.

text.p: Sri Lanka should take lessons in conflict resolution from Manila by involving separatists in the bid to end the island's ethnic conflict, a group of lawmakers has said.

The 22 lawmakers, from six political parties, submitted their proposal to a parliamentary committee studying a government plan aimed at ending the war between the government and Tamil rebels, Sarath Amunugama, of the main opposition United National Party (UNP), said on Monday.
"We suggested that the LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) be brought into any talks, at a time when we are possibly looking at a peace initiative," Amunugama told Reuters.

The group, which includes members of the ruling People's Alliance, made the suggestion after returning from the Philippines where group members observed conflict resolution practices by Manila and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) in their attempt to bring peace to Mindanao island.
The MNLF, the largest of the island's Moslem guerrilla groups, signed a peace accord with Manila in September after a 24-year-old battle.
But two rebel splinter groups, including the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), are still waging war against Manila despite nearly three years of negotiations.
"We thought the progress made by the Philippine government and the MNLF had brought about a positive stand to that conflict," Amunugama said.
"It was their initiative that made us appeal to our authorities to draw the LTTE to peace talks," he said.

The LTTE are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east. The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, now in its 14th year.
A peace plan proposed by Colombo is being debated by the parliamentary committee and is expected to be presented by November.
But the plan virtually ignores the LTTE, instead offering substantial devolution to minorities. It also counts on weakening the rebels militarily before negotiating with them.
Two previous peace initiatives, in 1990 and in 1994, failed.
